title: Total n00b, could use some insights, what a time to be alive.
author: ExhaustedDog
selftext:
Mostly a dreamer, no game dev nor coding experience, but have built a couple table top games for me and my friends and was an English teacher for a number of years, so I my background is certainly in building and scaffolding skill sets to take students through complex lessons at a pace that is challenging yet attainable.  
  
I've been tinkering and iterating on a die throwing game using Claude. Right now I've just been vibe coding the gameplay loop into an HTML for easy testing and to ensure systems are implemented in the way I want. It's also just as a thought experiment to see if the gameplay loop is even worth pursuing or just simply another slop game with no real merit or depth.

What's been helpful so far is being able to build the game to a state that is feature complete for that iteration, having Claude build a script to play through the game completely several times, and provide the raw gameplay data - such as how many runs/deaths (it's a roguelite) it would take, time spent clicking through menus (rather interesting and revealing metric I'll say), and number of direct player inputs and interactions - and an overall analysis.  
  
It help me realize fundamental design flaws when prompted to provide an in-depth evaluation design brief, highlighting the interactions between gameplay mechanics, and making recommendations of possible changes. This has been the most useful and illuminating aspect of development thus far, as it quickly identified how the core gameplay loop lacked any real and impactful player decisions and has since helped me refocus on core systems that make player decision branches, agency, and problem solving THE gameplay loop (instead of just building more ways to roll more die). Now it feels like I have a better pulse on how the ecosystem of systems should function with the underlying directive in place: make the player's decisions have a meaningful impact on what happens. 

Couple of areas that would be helpful:

1) Is my current method of developing the game a best practice or am I missing something entirely in these early stages?

2) If the game is built to such a state and the gameplay feels tight and unique enough from other games in the space, how would I want to proceed in terms of building visual assets, graphics, animations etc.?  (ideal end state would be 2.5d visuals, akin to Octopath Traveller II) What would my tech stack look like and are there any good tutorials out there you'd recommend to help me build an asset workflow? How does using AI even work with a game engine like Godot or Unity?

Appreciate the input and insights, it's amazing that this stuff is even possible, my 12 year old self skipping school to play FFVII could have never fathomed we'd be here.

comments.author: cxfoulke
comments.body:
As long as you avoid things like multiplayer, complex data.
AI can code and you can kind of forget about it now with the latest frontier models. 

However if you scope creep without an understanding of programming architecture and being able to very specifically prompt. Sometimes they get themselves into a big tangled mess. As long as scope remains relatively tight it'll be fine. 

Version control carefully though. Ask it to review the architecture and remove unneeded code. Simplify where possible etc. 

Data driven development is pretty good and normal. Strong test suites are normal and modern Ai will spam them. Although ai can sometimes confirm to the mean. Be careful relying to much on Ai for balance. Human Players pretty consistently don't trust/like true balance. 

For graphics and game engines Ai can do some of that for you... It can build a fully functional game in godot or unity without you needing to do a thing. 

But... AI art is still weak in a lot of areas. Ui it's pretty terrible at. Some folks will say you can do x or y and they might work with a limited scope. But after much experimenting at fighting with these systems your gonna have to either do alot yourself or pay for someone to make assets. Sound effects are also an Ai weak spot wanting something like an electric explosion sound or boxes clattering it's pay for it or so it yourself. They can do music although it will bring ai haters out of the walls to scream in your reviews. 

Anything ai art currently makes without some serious adjustments will make ai antis jump out of the walls at you. So learn it or pay for it. Ai art tools can speed you up a lot.

replies.author: snakesoul
replies.body: Excuse me, how is it possible for AI agents to make godot games without help? I mean, as far as I know, AI would help me with the scripting, but I would have to do all the "godot work" like creating scenes, rigidbodies, puting them together... Am I wrong? Thanks

replies.author: cxfoulke
replies.body:
modern models can do all of that without changing anything 

godot MCP will allow them to do it faster and cheaper on the token front. 

just ask with codex or claude code and they will do it not hard. Gets token pricey though.

replies.author: ExhaustedDog
replies.body: Sounds like Godot or Unity has an API that allows an AI to work directly in it? Or does the AI need to package the files to be then moved into the engine?

replies.author: cxfoulke
replies.body:
You just give it access to the folder and it can change any of the game files? 

Or you can mcp which does expose an API either or works. Mcp is just slightly cheaper on tokens. 

It's all automatic and simple

replies.author: ExhaustedDog
replies.body:
Yeah, learning how to be specific in prompts has been a learning curve for sure, especially when asked to complete more complex tasks that might take more than one session. Usually begin the next one with, continue coding where you left off on line XXXX.

Already experience version control when changing the names of classes, but it still wanted to reference the old classes on the back end and reasoned, "because it's not player facing" and I still made it change the code. I reasoned if that it might break something in the future if legacy conventions were still in the code and doing some legwork.

I wonder if I should start, when asking it to complete a play-through for testing to, deploy 5 different player strategies and provide the data and summary for each strategy. Could also help see if there's an ideal meta and to what extent it is better than other methods. Not saying having a meta build is game breaking as long as it operates withing the same standard deviation as the other approaches. No use building a class system with different abilities if there's ONE obvious choice that is significantly better than the others.

comments.author: EchoingAngel
comments.body:
Heavy planning up front will payoff a ton later on. Both with laying the proper foundation and helping prevent scope creep on the backend, as you thought of most things already (and worst case you force yourself to stick to the plan, unless the change is vital for the fun of the game, based on ACTUALLY playing it). Analytics and simulations, as you mentioned, are proving very useful for refining the trickier/more complex mechanics.



I don't find them great for new idea generation, ironically. My main weakness is technical know-how, but as far as how things should be, I (the human with tons of game playing experience) have to bring that to the table. It is great for telling what you want to happen and it figuring out HOW to make it happen, but as far as "what would be fun?", that's going to be as plain as YouTuber Claude scripts.



For assets, my game is 3D, so I can't directly comment on 2D or 2.5D, but Meshy, Tripo, and Rodin did alright for 3D assets once I had "perfect" pictures done, which I used ChatGPT for (it was a death march to get finalized images from the previous image model they had). Astra seems to be capable of sprite work, but you'd have to try it yourself.



For integration, the Unity MCP use with Codex has been quite a bump in technical ability. Though, again, they have no "taste", and nothing makes that more clear than UI development with them.

replies.author: ExhaustedDog
replies.body:
Good call out about being specific in what systems for it to look at in evaluating. And also that as experienced lifelong gamers we know what works and doesn't work, where we can decided to have maybe not the best in class systems without hurting the overall gameplay and experience.   
  
I've been extremely clear and specific with my prompts, and I always issue a directive when starting a new chat or project that all responses regarding game play mechanics or game states needs to operationally define so I can evaluate them on my own and decide if its good or bad.

And I agree that although its idea generation is limited, if I prompt it to base those recommendations on the interaction between the new system and one or two existing elements it at least gives me a starting point to work off of and consider. Especially so if I tell it to base those recommendations on the best standards within a genre or provide context for how specific games handle something similar, it's a bit trial and error. Sometimes my excitement of "oh this would be cool if..." just ends up being content bloat for the sake of cool without adding impact in the way I would have wanted. Not that having cool things is bad, but it's helpful to know when those cool things could be revised into an existing system that elevates instead of distracts players.

Thank you for the asset suggestions though, I'll for sure look into it.
